overview:
Kevala‑jñāna (Kevalajnana), often translated as “omniscience” or “absolute knowledge,” is one of the most central concepts in Jain epistemology and soteriology. It refers to the complete, infinite, and unobstructed cognition attained by a liberated soul (jīva) when all obscuring karmas—especially the jñānāvaraṇa (knowledge‑obscuring) karma—are fully destroyed. In Jain metaphysics, every soul inherently possesses infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. However, karmic bondage restricts these natural qualities. Kevala‑jñāna is the moment when the soul’s intrinsic omniscience manifests fully, without any limitation of space, time, object, or mode.

Across Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrti‑pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—Kevala‑jñāna is described as the highest form of knowledge, surpassing mati‑jñāna (sensory‑based cognition), śruta‑jñāna (scriptural knowledge), avadhi‑jñāna (clairvoyance), and manaḥparyāya‑jñāna (telepathy). It is attained only by those who reach the 13th guṇasthāna (stage of spiritual development), immediately preceding liberation (mokṣa). The omniscient being (kevalin) perceives all substances (dravya) and all their infinite modes (paryāya) simultaneously and directly.

Jain texts emphasize that Kevala‑jñāna is not a supernatural gift but the natural state of the soul once karmic veils are removed. It is also not equivalent to theistic omniscience; Jainism maintains a non‑theistic framework in which omniscience is a perfected state of any liberated soul, not a divine attribute of a creator deity. The attainment of Kevala‑jñāna marks the culmination of right faith (samyak‑darśana), right knowledge (samyak‑jñāna), and right conduct (samyak‑cāritra), collectively known as the three jewels (ratnatraya).

Descriptions of Kevala‑jñāna vary slightly across sects. Digambara texts often emphasize that a kevalin does not engage in verbal speech; instead, the divya‑dhvani (divine sound) emanates spontaneously. Śvetāmbara traditions describe omniscient beings as capable of speaking articulated words. Despite such differences, all traditions agree that Kevala‑jñāna represents perfect, infinite, and non‑erroneous knowledge, attained only through complete destruction of karmic bondage.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: When all knowledge‑obscuring karmas are destroyed, the soul becomes omniscient.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.1 is one of the most cited aphorisms defining Kevala‑jñāna. Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions accept this text, though commentaries differ in interpretation.

primary_sources.title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: The state of being a kevalin leads to the state of liberation.
primary_sources.notes: This canonical text associates omniscience directly with the final stage before mokṣa, emphasizing its soteriological significance.

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda lineage (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: Knowledge culminates in omniscience, and omniscience culminates in liberation.
primary_sources.notes: A foundational Digambara text describing the progressive purification of knowledge leading to Kevala‑jñāna.

primary_sources.title: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Śvetāmbara canonical text
primary_sources.translation: The omniscient one knows all things.
primary_sources.notes: This passage is frequently cited in Śvetāmbara tradition to illustrate the scope of omniscience.

misconceptions.myth: Kevala‑jñāna is a supernatural or miraculous power granted by a deity.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism teaches that omniscience is the natural state of every soul once karmic obstructions are removed. It is not bestowed by any external divine being.

misconceptions.myth: A kevalin knows only spiritual truths, not mundane details.
misconceptions.reality: Primary texts state that Kevala‑jñāna encompasses all substances and their infinite modes, including both spiritual and mundane realities.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain sects describe the kevalin identically.
misconceptions.reality: While all agree on the nature of omniscience, Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions differ on details such as whether a kevalin speaks verbally or emits divya‑dhvani.

misconceptions.myth: Kevala‑jñāna is equivalent to the omniscience of a creator god.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism is non‑theistic; omniscience is a perfected state of any liberated soul, not an attribute of a cosmic creator.
